Chapter 10: Lessons Unlearned
As the dust finally settled, the opioid crisis kept taking lives. Even as some things changed, new drugs showed up, new companies found ways to profit from pain, and that heartbreaking cycle of addiction and loss just kept spinning.
The Sacklers' story? It's just one chapter in a much bigger book—a story about how power, money, and ambition can reshape our world, sometimes for good, but just as often for harm.
Sure, a few reforms happened. Doctors got more careful with opioid prescriptions, regulators tightened some rules, and people started talking more openly about the risks. But let’s be honest—the real engines driving this crisis? The hunger for profit, the willingness to stretch the truth, and the sheer force of good marketing—they’re still out there.
Picture a doctor in a small-town clinic. She remembers every patient she’s lost to addiction. So, she tries to do things differently—she listens more, prescribes less, and spends time with families, working to rebuild trust. It’s tough. Sometimes, it doesn’t feel like enough. But for her, it’s a place to start.
For a lot of people, the Sackler story became a warning. It showed us what happens when the drive for success isn’t balanced by ethics or empathy—the damage can be devastating. And maybe, that’s the real lesson here: Lasting change will take more than new rules or stricter laws. It takes a real shift in our values, a willingness to ask those hard questions, and the guts to put people above profit.
The truth is, the legacy of the Sackler family is still being written. The pain they caused can’t be erased. But if we pay attention to the lessons from their story, maybe we can build something better, together.
